paragraphs: In the summer of Long’an’s fourth year, Xuyi once again smelled of roots boiled into pulp.

Two years earlier, when drought struck north of the Huai, Shanyang had opened its granaries and bought grain from Qin, while Xuyi had shut its gates and let refugees make their way north along the embankment. That year had left many houses empty. In spring, weeds had grown thick over the pits where the dead were buried beyond the south gate. Xuyi had a new governor now, but the past had not passed away. Once rebellion broke out in Kuaiji, military grain from several eastern commanderies was sent away in successive levies. Trading boats on the Huai were searched by river forts, and fewer captains were willing to carry provisions north. Half a month earlier an envoy from Jiankang had taken Xuyi’s last consignment of fine rice, claiming it was needed to suppress the rebels at Jingkou. Three days later the county withdrew its notice, only to announce a new requisition for military supplies after the autumn harvest.

Gu Chen had held office for less than a year. He climbed to the watchtower from behind the official residence and saw one roof south of the city without a thread of smoke. Two alleys away was another, and westward as far as the ward gate every kitchen hearth was cold. Two children sat beside a well clasping an empty earthen jar, waiting for someone to bring water from afar. When they caught sight of a bucket, they first stretched their hands toward the few grains of rice bran stuck to its bottom.
Inside the hall, the granary clerk was turning the old account pages with a furious rustle.
“The garrison has twelve days of grain. If we cut one meal, perhaps eighteen. The infirmary has already stopped receiving rations.”

Gu Chen ordered three bowls brought in. One held the local army’s grain, half a bowl of broken millet mixed with sand. The second contained powdered tree bark ground by poor households in the south of the city, so gray that its color could hardly be distinguished. The third was empty. When the granary clerk saw it, he lowered his head very far.
“Has Jiankang replied?” Gu Chen asked.
“The grain boats were requisitioned for the southeast. They say they will make good the amount after autumn.”
“How many people will still be here to collect it after autumn?”

No one answered. The people outside had been waiting all morning. Some brought land deeds to trade for food, the old paper damp, the red seals rubbed into stains. One person held a bronze mirror given by her mother at her wedding and offered it for half a dou. At first the city’s wealthy families had opened their doors to distribute relief twice or so; now they had strengthened their bolts so they need not see, day after day, the hands reaching through the cracks.

Gu Chen descended the hall steps and told the guards to open the prefectural gate. He went to see a woman collapsed beside the stone stairs. She was not dead. She had simply eaten nothing for days and lacked even the strength to lift her face. Gu ordered her carried to the infirmary, but the old physician there told him that some medicines could still be found; there was no porridge left.

Back at his desk, he found a copied report from two years before, when Du Qian of Shanyang had opened the granaries. The grain Du purchased had indeed reached the people, yet he had been accused of dealings with Qin. An officer of the Northern Garrison sent to escort him had released him on the road and later faced an inquiry under military law. Lu Yan of Xuyi had obeyed the edict to keep his gates shut and retained his office, but the city had lost much of its population. Gu Chen knew why his predecessors had gone wrong. He feared having to put his own brush to paper at precisely the same point.
“Is there grain left in the ever-normal granary at Xiacai?” he asked.
The chief clerk sprang up from his mat in alarm. “Governor, the Shanyang case is warning enough.”
“I know.”
“If Jiankang investigates, we shall—”
“You need not put your name to it.”

The chief clerk studied him, placed a hand against the desk, and sat down again. He had meant to say that culpability was not determined by the number of signatures. In the end he said nothing, but brought a thin bamboo tube and laid it on the table.

Gu Chen wrote two letters. One was a formal memorial to Jiankang, giving the actual figures for the military granaries and infirmary and requesting authority for emergency trade. The other bore no commandery seal and was entrusted to a merchant who knew the river, to be delivered to Xiacai. It contained no stirring appeal for aid, only terms: he wished to buy one hundred thousand shi of millet, twenty thousand in the first shipment. Qin soldiers must not escort the grain across the Huai, demand the surrender of the city, or change the people’s registration in exchange for the food. Whatever salt and cloth could be paid in advance would be paid; the remainder would be settled in installments from the commandery treasury. At the end he paused for a long time, but still signed his name.
“A private letter without a seal,” said the chief clerk. “Why should Qin believe it?”

From a torn cloth sack left by a shopkeeper, Gu Chen took a copper coin about the size of a fingertip, with rice husks clinging to it. Earlier someone outside the city had divided a sack of grain that had not yet been properly winnowed into more than ten portions, trading one for a piece of charcoal, until this was all that remained.
“Have the messenger carry this,” he said. “If the men at Xiacai ask what Xuyi has left, show it to them.”

The merchant left the city by night. His boat brushed the reeds, following the current for two days. The officials at Xiacai opened the bamboo tube, detained the messenger, and sent a fast boat to make discreet inquiries along the southern bank. When the report came back, the number of households lost to sickness and death was greater than Gu Chen had written. After much thought, the official sent both letters, together with the copper coin, to Chang’an.

When Fu Hong read the message, military offices outside were demanding provisions for the newly raised troops of Hebei. After years of disasters Hebei had only just begun to recover a little surplus, and each granary north of the Huai had its own frontier garrisons, camps of registered guests, and farming soldiers to feed. No one dared call one hundred thousand shi a trifling quantity. Quan Yi submitted two sets of figures. One showed the grain available without harming the army’s autumn needs; the other would require shipments to replenish it from Luoyang and Xuchang. The totals differed by more than forty thousand shi.
“With what will Gu Chen repay us?” Fu Jian asked.
“Salt and cloth, and next year’s land tax.”
“Will the same people still be working those fields next year?”

Fu Hong could not answer. He had seen several agreements mortgaging taxes yet to be collected. If warfare emptied a commandery of half its households, the more handsome the writing on such a contract, the more it resembled a demand for payment from the dead.

Fu Rong ordered the actual inventories from north of the Huai brought before him. He asked the frontier commander how much could be replaced after the rainy-season transport if twenty thousand shi were diverted. The old commander counted on his fingers until sweat stood on his forehead. They could preserve the garrison’s autumn rations, he said, but their winter stores would depend on the new millet reaching the granaries.
“Then dispatch twenty thousand shi first,” Fu Jian said. “No additional levies on the people to pay for it.”

One minister urged them to exchange grain for a city. Spreading out a map, he pointed to the embankment east of Xuyi and argued that three thousand elite horsemen could cross when the southern bank opened its granaries and seize the stronghold. Fu Rong did not rebuke him. He merely asked how much millet three thousand cavalry would consume each day after crossing, where they would stable their horses, and who would bring the final grain boat through. Before the minister had finished answering, no one was supporting him.

Fu Jian passed Gu Chen’s private letter around. The handwriting was cramped, water had stained the edges, and it had plainly been written in haste. After examining the copper coin, he ordered the Secretariat to amend the directive: twenty thousand shi were to be advanced at market value, with any further shipment subject to separate review. The other eighty thousand must not be entered as expenditure in the treasury accounts before they were provided. Only boatmen, account keepers, and physicians might travel aboard; troops were to stop on the northern bank. Each grain sack would have an official granary seal inside its fastening, but no Qin banner displayed outside.
At first Quan Yi objected. “If there are no official marks, how will we verify a shortage?”

“Keep the seal inside, and cut it open in front of both sides at handover,” Fu Hong said. “If they destroy the outer document on the southern bank, the account will not be destroyed with it. Each side makes a copy, and another stays north of the Huai.”

Fu Jian agreed. The Secretariat drew up the contract; the grain officers of Xuchang and Luoyang were jointly responsible for losses. This was neither a gift of grain nor an offering of a city. At the foot of the order the officials wrote only names, quantities, dates for repayment, and the day beyond which the boats must not advance.

Others on the southern bank had also received Gu Chen’s appeal. Zhu Xu was staying at an old friend’s house in Jingkou, searching old Xiangyang casualty rolls for the name of a sick soldier. More than two years had passed since he returned south from Chang’an. Repeatedly questioned by the Jin court, he held no active post. He recognized Gu Chen’s handwriting, and knew that here was a man laying his own head upon the execution block before the case against him had even begun.

He took the letter to the military headquarters to find Liu Yu. Liu was outside the army granary, his sleeves streaked with wet ash as he ordered soldiers to turn moldy sacks over to dry. After reading what Gu had written, he did not ask how much grain Qin could provide. His first question was, “How many people are still in Xuyi who have not fled?”
“Fewer than two years ago, but there are more sick.”
“Who gave them leave to buy grain from the north?”
“No one.”

Liu Yu slowly folded the letter, and Zhu Xu thought he would refuse. Instead Liu called for the registers of the Jingkou garrison boats, found the river force recently assigned to the Huai, and marked several dozen vessels.
“The court has ordered me to patrol the Huai and stop Qin soldiers from crossing secretly,” Liu Yu said. “If this is grain and nothing else, we shall first establish whether it is grain.”
Zhu Xu asked, “And if someone orders you to burn it on the river?”
“I must first receive an order before I can say whose order I shall obey.”
“And if it does come?”

Liu Yu raised his eyes to him. “Master Zhu, you are asking for grain on behalf of the south and a guarantee on behalf of the north. I can promise you only this: my military report will record what my inspection finds.”

Zhu did not press further. He requested permission from the Qin frontier authorities to act as a civilian guarantor on the southern side and cross with the grain boats, without accepting any Qin seal or office. Fu Hong granted it in writing, explicitly stating that Zhu would not be under Qin military command. If the Jin court detained him, Chang’an could only negotiate under existing frontier agreements; the grain-escort cavalry would not be permitted to cross on their own initiative. Reading the reply, Zhu laughed that father and son of the Fu house had become even fonder of annotations than in years past. He packed his belongings into a single cloth bundle.

The river rose in the sixth month, and grain boats gathered at Xiacai. More than two hundred flat-bottomed craft crowded the bend. Granary clerks counted sacks boat by boat, cut the inner seals, verified them, and affixed fresh seals from both parties. Watching the water creep higher through the night, boatmen cursed the need to weigh every shi of rice three times. The escort officer cursed as well, saying the officials would rather watch the grain go moldy in the boats than let him take even a squad of armed men along.

As Zhu Xu boarded the leading vessel, a group of Qin soldiers were helping to carry medicine chests onshore. Several old veterans recognized the former defender of Xiangyang and called out, “General Zhu!” He turned and clasped his hands in acknowledgment, but did not take the military banner they offered him.

Sailing east along the Huai, the boats gradually made out a dark mass of people on the southern bank. They stood along the embankment without shouting. First a Jin standard rose from the reeds, then the tall masts of warships. Liu Yu stood at the front in armor and commanded the convoy to halt.
“Inspect the boats.”
Zhu Xu asked, “And when you are done?”
“We shall decide when we are done.”
“Have you an order from Jiankang forbidding them?”
“There is an existing order against carrying weapons into our territory without leave. I will inspect under that order. As for the rest, I shall answer when I know.”

Northern Garrison soldiers went aboard, lifting hatch boards and opening sacks with their spear points. One young man scooped a handful of millet and first brought it to his nose, then quietly put a few grains in his mouth. His squad leader slapped his fingers away. Liu Yu saw it but did not reprimand him. He remembered that the same soldier had asked the headquarters for food for his sick mother the previous month. The grain clerk had told him the accounts were not yet reconciled and he must wait three days.

When the last boat had been searched, they had found only rice, medicines, cloth, and bundled rolls of records. A government document attached to the accounts declared the grain to have come from Qin territory as a loan to Xuyi at market price. The Northern Garrison’s deputy commander wanted to throw the paper into the river and detain the vessels midstream.
Liu Yu asked him, “If you keep these boats here for three days, what condition will the grain be in?”
“Better that than letting the Qin into the city.”
“I asked about the grain.”

The deputy turned away without answering. Suddenly someone shouted from the southern bank. An old woman holding a child ran into the shallows and knelt where the mud covered her knees. A shore guard tried to drag her back, but she clung desperately to a floating plank. Some on the boats could not bear to watch and threw her an old coil of rope. She caught it just before the current carried her away.

Liu Yu ordered the medicine chests checked and the boatmen’s identities verified, then summoned Xuyi’s granary clerk to examine the accounts face to face. The clerk had brought no commandery seal, and Gu Chen himself had not arrived. Both sides waited stubbornly until evening. Zhu Xu stood at the bow from noon until the sun sank into the reeds and never once urged them to hurry, afraid that any urging would make it look still more as though he were pressing the Jin army on Fu Jian’s behalf.

At last Gu Chen arrived in a skiff. He was so thin that his cheekbones stood out. He carried the official seal in his sleeve and had only the chief clerk beside him. He bowed deeply to Liu Yu; when he saw Zhu Xu aboard, he hesitated. The Jin general who had once defended Xiangyang was now bringing the two banks together over a grain agreement. Loyalty and treason were no longer words that could easily settle the matter.
“Is that seal genuine?” Liu Yu asked.
“It is.”
“Who stands responsible for the grain debt?”
“The treasury of Xuyi. If the treasury cannot meet it, I pledge my own property first.”

Liu regarded him for a moment, then ordered the granary clerk to affix the commandery seal in public, alongside the separate Qin accounts. Beside them he countersigned: vessels inspected; no weapons or armor found; unloading authorized under the grain agreement, with distribution supervised by the Northern Garrison. Someone muttered that the old Du Qian case still hung over Liu’s head, and now he was adding another. Liu heard him and simply told a clerk to dry the ink.

Before dark the first grain boat struck the wooden piles of the landing. Starving people surged forward. For a moment Northern Garrison soldiers drew their swords, but Liu shouted for spears to be lowered and shields used to hold back the crowd. The medicine chests were to be unloaded first, the sick carried next. A child found a few kernels of raw millet spilled beside the boat. He rubbed away the husks and was about to swallow them when Zhu Xu hurried to stop him and told a physician to cook thin porridge, so that those who had long gone hungry could take food gently. The child would not unclench his fist. Four grains were pressed so tightly within it that his knuckles turned white.

At dawn the next day, smoke began rising in slender threads above Xuyi’s roofs. Gu Chen stood beside a temporary grain shed, personally checking the first wooden ration tokens. The steward of an estate, his clothes still neat and clean, presented a sealed document claiming a hundred shi on the ground that his household sheltered more than thirty tenant families. Gu ordered him to bring those families one by one. The steward flew into a rage, saying the governor suspected great clans of concealing households. Gu made no further reply. He sent two clerks to verify the count at the estate. He could issue that order, not because he had suddenly ceased to fear the powerful families, but because Northern Garrison soldiers stood at the granary doors and Liu Yu’s name appeared in the accounts.

Xu Sanniang was among those in line. Two years earlier she had carried her feverish, unconscious young son from outside Xuyi’s walls to the northern bank and had not dared come south again until winter. The boy could stand on his own now, though he had suffered in the cold and still coughed frequently. The pay owed to Xu Cheng for defending the city had never been settled in full. When the granary clerk asked for her household name, she pushed the child gently ahead and told him to say it himself. He spoke very softly, then took hold of his mother’s robe.

When her turn came, only half a dou of broken grain remained in the wooden measure. Xu Sanniang did not strike the desk. She asked first when the next boat would arrive. The clerk said afternoon. She tied the half dou into a cloth bag and took her child to wait at a corner of the city. If no boat came that afternoon, she would have to ask once more.
Zhu Xu came down from the boat and saw Liu Yu folding a Secretariat notice, removing the page that bore Qin’s reign title.
“Going to tear it up?” Zhu asked.
“Going to put it away.”
“The figures in that document are true.”

“And they remain in both sets of accounts. The notice on the wall will say only how much is issued today and where people can collect their share tomorrow. First they must be able to recognize their own wooden tokens.”

Zhu watched the people in the line. One old soldier held half a bowl of watery porridge, shifting it from hand to hand because it burned his fingers, yet unable to stop lowering his head to drink. White paste stained the corners of his mouth. Zhu recognized the beard: the man had once stood with him defending an arrow tower on Xiangyang’s walls. Now the veteran neither greeted him nor avoided his eyes. He simply cupped the bowl against his breast, taking great care not to spill it.
The two men walked a while along the embankment. Liu Yu asked, “Which side were you acting for?”
Zhu pulled his outer robe tight as the river wind made him cough twice.
“I boarded a Qin boat from the southern bank and came back to the southern bank again. I have old comrades on either shore, and each fears that I will carry off the other’s secrets.”
“What did you carry?”
“A letter from an official surnamed Gu who was born in Xuyi and wanted to see Xuyi’s children live until next year.”

Liu Yu asked no more. Both knew that Qin grain came at a cost. It saved lives, but afterward the commanderies along the Huai could no longer pretend that the north contained only horses and blades. By allowing the boats into port, Liu had also guaranteed Gu Chen’s action outside the military order. These matters would look very ugly in Jiankang’s official records.

When the grain boats had been emptied, Gu Chen said that another eighty thousand shi remained to be arranged with the Qin court. Liu Yu told him to settle the accounts of the first shipment before discussing the next, lest later entries become impossible to reconcile. Exhausted, Gu could only nod. Before boarding the vessel that would take him back, Zhu Xu gave Liu an old register he had brought from Jiangnan: the surviving fragments of the list of households that had left Xuyi two years before. Many of their names now appeared again in the grain distribution rolls.
“They have come back?” Liu asked.
“Some have. Some have not. And the children who stayed on the northern bank have grown older.”

Liu turned to one entry: a household originally recorded as three persons, then corrected in small red characters to four. At the end was written, “Newborn daughter, not yet named.” He closed the register, and for reasons he could not explain it weighed more heavily on him than a whole report of glorious battles.

A stern edict from Jiankang arrived soon afterward. It ordered an investigation into Gu Chen’s unauthorized purchase of Qin grain and commanded Liu Yu to seal the remaining stores pending the court’s decision. When the envoy came, the fires under the city’s porridge pots had not yet gone out. Liu did not tear up the edict. He wrote a reply listing, item by item, the quantity of grain, the number of boats, those sick or dead, and the remaining stores, signing it himself at the end. He told the envoy to take back one of that morning’s wooden porridge tokens, so that the men in Jiankang might also see whose hands received a dou of rice that day.

The vessels on the north bank had already returned empty. The landing lay in disarray: wet hemp rope, broken wooden ladles, and scattered millet husks mingled in the mud. Liu Yu kept watch in his cloak all night. Near dawn he saw a few children crowding around a stove, scrambling for warmth and saying the words “Qin grain.” He did not correct them. He merely ordered the cooking pot set firmly on its stand again.
